title: LESSON 1: WORD ORDER IS THE RULE

content: English has almost no word endings.
The ORDER of the words does the work:
who acts first, then the action, then
the rest.
I have it.    (I + have + it)       Press 1
Tom has it. (same order, new name)  Press 2
Nouns never change for their job, and
things have no he/she. Only I/me, he/him
swap when they swap place.
The grammar rides on little helper words
- be, do, will - that step in as we go.
Your language may show who-does-what a
different way; English uses position.

title: LESSON 2: TO BE AND THE PRONOUNS

content: 'To be' is the verb that changes shape
most by person:
I am                                Press 1
you are                             Press 2
he is / she is / it is              Press 3
we are / they are                   Press 4
Know these six as whole forms. Subject
pronouns open the sentence: I, you, he,
she, it, we, they. One 'you' serves all,
one or many, friend or stranger.
Apostrophes and Abbreviation: (joining words)
I'm; you're; she's; it's; they're   Press 5
Your language may split 'you' or skip
'be'; English keeps one of each.

pronunciation_mappings.3: He is. She is. It is.

content: English spelling is an accident of history,
not always a useful guide to pronunciation.
Let the audio recordings guide you.
Listen, then copy what you hear.
LEARNING TO SAY 'TH'
Hold the tip of your flattened tongue between
your front teeth. Feel the resistance of the
air passing by. Experiment with pressure and
tongue position. Push out into a vowel sound.
It won't take long to get it right.
Thor thought things through thoroughly   Press 1
The nearest sound in your language is
close but not the same; 'TH' is the sound
of air rushing past your tongue and teeth.
Three little words flag a noun:
a / an  = any one, new to us
the     = the one we both know
I see a man. (some man, first time)   Press 1
I see the man. (the man we mean)      Press 2
Choose 'a' or 'an' based on the SOUND:
an apple, an hour (silent h)          Press 3
a terminal, a house                   Press 4
Article systems differ across languages;
learn English's by the ear, from the audio.
English builds new verbs from a small
verb plus a small particle:
get + up    = get up    (leave bed)   Press 1
go + on     = go on     (happen)      Press 2
come + back = come back (return)      Press 3
The pair is ONE word - learn it whole.
The particles - up, out, back, on, off,
over - repaint one verb after another.
Watch out: the meaning is often NOT the
parts added up. 'go on' is not go + on;
it means 'happen'.
Your language builds such verbs its own
way; line that up with this machine.
Four words point at things - near or far,
one or many:
NEAR: This one, these ones (plural)   Press 1
I have this. I have these.            Press 2
FAR: That one, those ones (plural)    Press 3
I see that. I want those.             Press 4
'That' also answers back: 'That's it!'
= what you said is right.
All four open with a soft TH - the same
tongue as in 'think', but voiced. Say: this.
Two ranks or three? English points just
two ways: near and far.

pronunciation_mappings.2: I have this. I have these.
pronunciation_mappings.4: I see that. I want those.

content: Some words do social work that grammar
cannot. Use them as ready-made frames:
please     - rides a request
sorry      - opens a repair
thank you  - closes it
Come here, please.                  Press 1
Sorry, I can't.                     Press 2
Thank you so much.                  Press 3
Quick replies too: okay, sure, yes, no.
Weight matters: 'Come here' is an order;
add 'please' and it becomes a request.
Every language softens its own way;
in English these words do it.
English loves to reuse one small form
for several ideas. Nearly half of these
1000 words carry such a split:
time  = the clock, AND 'one more time'
back  = a direction, AND a body part
right = a side, AND 'correct'
Each card pins just ONE meaning. The
example sentence is your anchor - read
the sentence, not the bare word.
When a second meaning matters, the Notes
name it. Often it returns later as its
own card.
In your language these usually split into
separate words; here one form does both.
The everyday tense for what is usually
true. The verb keeps ONE shape for I,
you, we, they - and adds -s for he,
she, it:
I work. You work. We work. They work.
He works. She works. It works.      Press 1
That -s carries two sounds you can hear:
works - a hissing /s/               Press 2
comes - a buzzing /z/, the voice on    Press 3
After a hissing sound, add -es: one extra beat.
This tense means always or usually true,
not what is happening right now.
Your language may mark the person on
every verb; English marks only he/she/it.

pronunciation_mappings.1: He works. She works. It works.

content: How English says that something exists:
there is  + ONE thing
there are + MANY things
There is a house here.              Press 1
There is someone at home.           Press 2
There are two houses here.          Press 3
There are two girls in the house.   Press 4
In speech: there's a house (= there is).
This 'there' is not the place-word 'there'
(over there) - one form, two jobs (see
Lesson 8).
Your language may use one fixed word for
both; English changes is/are for number.

pronunciation_mappings.4: There are two girls in the house.

content: To show who owns a thing, the OWNER
takes a small mark: 's.
my father's name                    Press 1
the man's home                      Press 2
Anna's day                          Press 3
To SAY you own it, use have or have got
(same meaning, everyday speech):
I have a home. = I have got a home.    Press 4
Short form: I've got a home.
He has got a name. = He's got a name.
Your language may put the owner after the
thing, or show it with an ending, not 's.

pronunciation_mappings.4: I have a home. I have got a home.

content: Meet English's most important helper:
the auxiliary DO / DOES.
It carries the person and the time, so
the main verb can stay plain.
For emphasis, you drop it in:
I DO like it!   She DOES know you.  Press 1
You already hear it in set questions:
Do you want it? Do you know my dad?    Press 2
Plain 'do a thing' (I do my work) is a
different job - the same little word.
Full questions and negatives come later.
Your language may just change word order
or tone to ask; English adds do.

pronunciation_mappings.1: I DO like it! She DOES know you.
pronunciation_mappings.2: Do you want it? Do you know my dad?
